entities.name: Arsacius of Tarsus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Arsacius of Tarsus, installed as Archbishop of Constantinople in March 404 CE, served a brief but tumultuous tenure until his death on November 12, 405 CE. Elevated to the patriarchal see at an advanced age, approximately eighty years old, Arsacius's appointment was a direct consequence of the political machinations surrounding the deposition of his predecessor, John Chrysostom. His brief episcopacy, occurring amidst the escalating theological and political struggles of the late Roman Empire, highlights the profound influence of imperial power on ecclesiastical appointments and the deep schisms within the early Christian Church.

His elevation was orchestrated by Emperor Arcadius and Empress Aelia Eudoxia, who sought a pliant figure to replace the outspoken John Chrysostom, exiled for his criticisms of the imperial court and clergy. Despite being Chrysostom's elder brother, Arsacius lacked his sibling's popular support and theological gravitas, leading to widespread condemnation from Chrysostom's loyal followers, known as the Johannites. Many orthodox clergy and laypeople refused to recognize his authority, leading to a significant schism within the Constantinopolitan church, with congregations often boycotting his services and holding their own separate liturgies.

The schism initiated by Arsacius's controversial appointment persisted for years after his death, profoundly destabilizing the capital's ecclesiastical landscape and contributing to the broader theological disputes of the 5th century. His tenure, though short, became a stark illustration of the imperial court's capacity to dictate religious leadership, thereby influencing doctrinal adherence and congregational loyalty within the burgeoning Christian world. The resistance to Arsacius underscored the growing importance of popular and clerical consent in episcopal elections, even in the face of imperial decree.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Arsacius's brief tenure as Archbishop of Constantinople, though personally uneventful, became a focal point for the deep schisms between imperial power and ecclesiastical independence, leading to a lasting division within the capital's church. His appointment highlighted the political vulnerabilities of the early Christian leadership and the enduring influence of John Chrysostom.
